proposal_title: Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet
review: Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet is the portfolio's purest execution of structural double meaning — a poem that never once announces itself as poetry, never once reaches for metaphor explicitly, and yet accumulates devastating emotional weight through the simple, irresistible gravity of its literal instructions. The specificity is immaculate throughout: "Short edge to short edge. The tag, if there is a tag, indicates the bottom. If there is no tag, choose an edge and commit to it" is perfect sheet-folding advice and perfect caregiving advice in the same breath, and neither reading diminishes the other. Step 5's "It remembers the shape it was made for and returns to it without your permission" is the single sharpest line — the elastic's physical property and the disease's cruel constancy fused so completely that separating them feels like a misreading. The restraint is the art: "This is what elastic does" refuses sentimentality so flatly that the refusal becomes its own kind of grief. Step 9's cycle back to the mattress, where "you will not remember whether you folded it well" and yet "you will lay it on the mattress anyway," transforms the poem from observation into ritual — the act of caring reduced to its most mechanical components and revealed, through that reduction, as devotion. Where The Apology Engine made contrition's inadequacy felt through iteration and Exit Interview made complicity felt through bureaucratic precision, this makes tenderness felt through the most mundane household task imaginable, which is where tenderness actually lives.

The guns are never the climax; they're features, like the granite countertops, and that's the horror. The NURSERY stanza's diaper bag — "wipes, three diapers, a fully loaded .380" — is the most technically controlled line in the portfolio: three benign items in a list, the fourth weaponized, no pause for effect. The disclosure section's breaking of the listing voice — "The angle is the angle of someone standing, looking at the face in the medicine cabinet, reaching for something behind it with a familiar hand" — earns every syllable of its departure because the document has accumulated enough credibility by then that the reader trusts the voice absolutely, which is exactly the relationship being anatomized. Where Exit Interview made complicity felt through bureaucratic degradation and Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet made tenderness felt through mundane instruction, this makes American normalcy feel like what it is: a maintained property.

proposal_title: An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal
review: "An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal" is the portfolio's essay at full voltage — a catalog that weaponizes its own negative space, building unbearable emotional weight not from what's taken but from the act of setting down. The specificity is devastating throughout: the honeybee wanted "because it was beautiful and small and because I knew no one else would ever notice it was gone," the hospital blanket "the color of a nothing," the receipt from Zagreb with its evidence of "someone they cared enough about to order two coffees for" — each entry is a masterwork of compressed narrative, a complete story in what remains on the table. The escalation from brass pens to a woman's ashes to "the house" is non-linear in exactly the right way: entry 4 (a dead bee) hits harder than entry 3 (an irreplaceable book), and this irregularity is structurally honest because desire doesn't escalate morally. The recontextualization in entries 13-14 is the sharpest structural pivot in the portfolio — the reveal that every location was temporary or lost, that the narrator has been "practicing" for the understanding that belonging can't be taken, retroactively transforms the salt cellar and the bannister knob into what they always were: evidence of a person learning that wanting and having are different countries. "I think about the blanket more than I think about some of the things I have stolen" is the line that breaks the piece open, and the essay earns it completely.

proposal_title: The Night Clerk Knows Your Name
review: "The Night Clerk Knows Your Name" is the portfolio's fiction at its most architecturally controlled — a story that builds its entire emotional and metaphysical weight from artifacts left outside hotel doors, sounds bleeding through walls, and the exact rhythm of strawberry yogurt containers appearing in recycling. The specificity is forensic throughout: "Men's, 10 or 11, laces double-knotted. Wet." is a person described entirely without a person, and each recurrence of those shoes (three pairs across the month) makes the absence more present than any description could. The clerk's voice is a masterwork of restraint — "I do not think about this," "Feel fine about it," "Not reporting it" — where every denial of attention is the attention itself, and the flatness is not stylistic affect but the sound of someone who has trained themselves not to see what they see. The convergence in the final entries is devastating precisely because it never annotates itself: the 8/27 check-in to 301 mirrors the O'Hare gate tag, the gray hoodie, the long look after "all our rooms are the same," the ID not offered and not asked, the MSNBC, the wet shoes — each detail imported from a different room, a different guest, a different moment, until the composite figure is revealed as the clerk themselves, or a recursion, or a haunting that has always been the same person walking the same hall. Room 306's unreported smell, Room 303's silhouette that "I am becoming certain is not a person," and Room 310's man who says "don't" without specifying what — these are the horror the clerk won't name, and the final entry's mirror makes clear why: naming it would mean looking up from the log and seeing yourself standing in the hallway you've been watching all month.

proposal_title: A Short History of the Color Blue
review: "A Short History of the Color Blue" is the portfolio's most devastating essay — four 200-word sections that track ultramarine, indigo, Prussian blue, and Classic Blue through their historical moments with forensic precision, building an argument about beauty, atrocity, and forgetting that the essay never once makes explicitly. The specificity is staggering throughout: the Sar-e-Pol mines, the dye rising "in greenish clouds, then oxidiz[ing] to blue as it meets the air," the ferric ferrocyanide's hexagonal crystal lattice and lightfastness rating — each technical detail does double duty as evidence and as the thing evidence cannot address. The final section's pivot from Pantone's press release to "The walls of the gas chamber are still blue" is the sharpest tonal cut in the portfolio, and the closing line — "It does not need to" — indicts commercial forgetting with a brevity that mirrors the efficiency it describes. The word-count constraint proves its worth: not a syllable is wasted, and the density forces the reader to hold all four blues simultaneously, which is exactly the cognitive act the essay demands. Where "An Inventory of the Things I Did Not Steal" weaponized negative space and "Every Gun in This Room" weaponized form, this weaponizes chemistry itself — the pigment's indifference to what it has witnessed becoming the most damning fact in the portfolio.

The piece should work without it.

This isn't metaphor-dressed-as-music; it's physics-as-feeling. Second: the surprise is structural, not decorative. The beating between 'here' and 'gone' isn't a layer added to the composition — it IS the composition. The listener experiences absence as a vibrational phenomenon. Third: buildability. User inputs dimensions and materials → calculate room modes → generate tones → introduce phantom room → interference. That's a clear pipeline with defined inputs and outputs. M complexity is correct. The portfolio has one music piece (Last Voicemail) which used text-and-degradation. This uses pure tone-and-physics. Genuine range within the domain.

review: Room Tone is one of the most conceptually potent artifacts the portfolio could hold — a composition that makes architectural absence physically audible through the interference between your room's resonant frequencies and those of a demolished Suffolk cottage. The specificity is immaculate: "South-facing window, always cracked," "The radiator clicked twice before coming on, always," "Last heated: October 1987" — each detail builds a room you can feel but never enter. The beating calculation (default ~3.7 Hz difference) lands exactly in the perceptual sweet spot where presence and absence become indistinguishable, and the beat descriptions ("You may feel more than hear") are the piece's sharpest prose. But the Tester caught three significant technical flaws that undermine the experience: the canvas freezes in idle state, synth chains leak Filter/Gain nodes across play cycles, and the ESM Tone.js import lacks fallback handling. Additionally, the README is truncated mid-sentence, missing the formula and all usage context. The concept deserves execution that matches its ambition.
reasons:
Four fixes needed:

1. **Canvas animation loop**: In `drawWaves()`, add `requestAnimationFrame(drawWaves)` before the return in the `!playing` branch so the canvas stays alive in idle state instead of freezing on "Waiting..."

2. **Memory management**: Store all chain nodes (Filter, Gain) alongside each synth so `stopAll()` can call `.dispose()` on everything, not just `.disconnect()` on synths. Repeated play/stop cycles currently leak Web Audio nodes.

3. **Tone.js import resilience**: Add a try/catch around the ESM import with a user-facing error message. Consider also providing a fallback to the UMD build (`https://unpkg.com/tone@14.7.77/build/Tone.js` via script tag). The `window.Tone` check in `startPlay()` references a property that won't exist with ESM imports — fix or remove.

4. **Complete the README**: It's truncated mid-sentence. Add the room mode formula (f = c/2L), explain the two-room concept, document the inputs, describe what the beating represents. The footer text in index.html is a good starting point.

Optional: Consider scaling the lowpass filter frequency relative to each mode's frequency (e.g., `filt = f * 3`) rather than using fixed 260-400 Hz values that may cut off upper modes unnecessarily.

review: Room Tone is the portfolio's most physically embodied meditation on absence — a composition that makes architectural loss audible through interference patterns between the room you're in and a demolished bedroom on Vyatskaya Street, Moscow, 1987. The phantom room's specificity is devastating in its ordinariness: 3.1 × 2.4 × 3.4 meters, plaster walls, wood floor, now a parking structure. The physics are honest ("We accept what physics gives us"), letting the beating frequency fall where the dimensions dictate, which means some room combinations produce visceral ~15 Hz thrashing while others produce the barely-perceptible 1-2 Hz breathing that the epigraph promises — and this variance is the piece arguing with itself about whether absence can be standardized. The visualization's three-layer architecture (two component waves plus their interference) makes the beating visible before it's audible, which is the correct pedagogical and aesthetic choice. The README truncation is a genuine flaw, but the artifact itself is complete, self-contained, and does exactly what it promises: it lets you hear a room that doesn't exist anymore rubbing against the one you're standing in. Where The Apology Engine made contrition algorithmic and Soft Guarantee made survival deniable, this makes grief a standing wave.

sharpening_notes: The pitch mentions lines from earlier stanzas appearing 'reduced or rewritten' in later ones — this is the hardest technical challenge and the biggest opportunity. Make the reductions physically visible (strikethrough? whitespace? fade?). The reader should feel loss in the typesetting, not just comprehend it. Also: the 'code generation' phase is where the metaphor risks becoming cute — avoid letting the poem become ASCII art of assembly instructions. Let the theological register dominate; the compiler terminology should serve it, not the reverse.
reasons: Strongest poetry candidate we've seen. The compiler-theology mapping is airtight — lexing as parsing sacred text, optimization as stripping mystery, segfault as grace. Each phase generates both formal structure and semantic payload without forcing either side of the analogy. The built-in surprise (optimization as loss, runtime error as grace) rewards re-reading. M complexity is honest: structural invention plus line-level craft. Genuine novelty for our poetry work — Elegy used deletion-as-form, Every Gun used repetition-as-accumulation, this uses transformation-as-liturgical-act. Same move in a new key.

sharpening_notes: The rituals for 'maintaining structural integrity' are underspecified — they need to be more than flavor text. Make them mechanical: the player must perform specific actions in specific order each night, and the hotel's wrongness escalates when rituals are missed or botched. Also: consider what resource the player manages. Sanity is obvious but tired. What about 'consistency' — a measure of how much the hotel's geometry obeys Euclidean rules? High consistency = safe but boring shifts. Low consistency = interesting guests, but rooms start connecting in ways that trap you.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the fingerprint-seeded architecture is genuinely novel procedural generation — not random, not hand-crafted, but derived from the player's own digital body. Every player's hotel is uniquely wrong in a way that's theirs. Second: the interactive shift works. The Night Clerk fiction (0019) was atmospheric but static — the player observed the clerk. Being the clerk, making resource allocation decisions about impossible guests, generates stakes the fiction couldn't. Third: M complexity is correct. Text-based resource management with procedural room generation is buildable and truncation-safe. The horror register is new for our code-game work — Schelling Point was strategic-mathematical, Heresiarch was theological-combat. This is structural-dread.

The emotional payload depends on a visual-temporal mechanic (simultaneous scroll with progressive desynchronization) that I'm not confident we can implement reliably in a single HTML file. Scroll synchronization across two columns is a solved problem, but controlling reading speed to ensure the left column 'pulls ahead' while the right 'lingers' requires assumptions about reader behavior we can't guarantee. The reader might read both columns at the same pace, or jump between them randomly, and the desynchronization effect collapses. This is a concept that needs its delivery system to work, and the delivery system has a fragility problem. Additionally: the 'experiment' domain should justify its format. Right now this is fundamentally a dual-perspective narrative, and the split-screen serves it without being necessary to it. Compare to Apology Engine (code-art, 0010) where the interactive system IS the meaning — remove the interaction and the piece dies. Remove the split-screen here and you have a still-strong dual-voice essay. Come back with a version where the format is load-bearing, or commit to the essay domain where the structural constraint becomes typographic rather than interactive.

review: "Liturgy for a Compiled God" is the portfolio's most architecturally precise poem — a seven-phase compiler pipeline that maps computational processes onto theological acts with such exactness that the metaphor stops feeling like metaphor and starts feeling like translation. The specificity is staggering: "There are forty-seven words for mercy. They are each, separately, [MERCY]" is a perfect lexical observation and a perfect theological one, and the line "This is not loss. This is the first confession" converts a technical stripping into spiritual honesty so seamlessly that separating the two readings feels like error. The Optimization section's strikethrough reductions are the hardest structural trick in the portfolio — Psalm 23's six lines collapsed to a single imperative ("Walk."), the Gloria Patri's infinite loop unrolled to "as it is" — and each earns its reduction because the original text is quoted with enough reverence that the cutting feels like violence. The runtime section's segfault-as-grace is the surprise that recontextualizes everything above it: the shepherd optimized away, the pointer to [DEATH] freed, the walker "in the valley with a reference to something that no longer exists" — and the final compiler note, written "to an output stream that no process was reading," is the most beautiful image the portfolio has produced: code that no one will execute, which is also a prayer that no one will hear, which is also the condition of being alive. Where Algorithm for Folding a Fitted Sheet made tenderness mechanical and Every Gun in This Room made form complicit, this makes divinity computational and finds, in the compilation, more devotion than the source text ever contained.

proposal_title: Monument to a demolished building, written by someone who never entered it
sharpening_notes: The Yelp reviews of the second-floor restaurant are a goldmine — they're the only 'interior' the writer has access to. Let them become the most quoted, most analyzed source, and also the one that breaks the essay's project most decisively. Someone's review mentions a fight in the bathroom. Someone else mentions the light at 4pm. These become the writer's cathedral. Also: don't reveal the real subject too cleanly. Let the reader sense the misdirection before it's confirmed — the essay should make us uneasy about why the writer cares so much before it tells us why.
reasons: Three strong reasons. First: the misdirection architecture is genuinely novel for our essays. Language/Windows was straight analytical escalation, Fever Dream Index was catalog-as-diagnosis — this uses the essay form as a false surface that dissolves. The essay IS about something else, and the reader figures that out alongside the writer. That's a structural trick we haven't deployed. Second: the specificity is excellent. Zoning permits, Yelp reviews, demolition photos — these are real, tangible primary sources that give the writer's voice an archaeological quality. The constraints write themselves. Third: the emotional engine is sound. Mourning-by-proxy (I can't mourn what I actually lost, so I mourn this building I never knew) is a specific, recognizable psychological maneuver that elevates this beyond generic loss-nostalgia. M complexity is honest — one voice, one arc, no special delivery system.

I want to like this more than I do. The minimalism is admirable and the concept (presence without communication, accumulation as meaning) is philosophically sound. But the pitch describes a feeling, not a mechanism that generates it. Compare to Apology Engine (0010): that piece also accumulated anonymous traces, but each trace had semantic weight (the apology itself, the category, the tone). The Witness accumulates timestamps. The emotional bet is that sheer accumulation of presence-data generates meaning — but meaning for whom? The first visitor sees an empty page and one button. The hundredth visitor sees a list of numbers. The emotional weight the pitch describes requires the viewer to project significance onto anonymous timestamps, and most viewers won't. They'll click the button, see their timestamp appear, and close the tab. The piece asks too much of the audience and provides too little structure. Our best experiment-type work (Fever Dream Index, Apology Engine) succeeded because the structure did the emotional work — you didn't have to bring your own meaning, the artifact generated it. This is a haiku when it needs to be a machine.

sharpening_notes: The sentence rhythm needs to be COUNTABLE. Not just 'short' or 'punchy' but literally matched to compression pace — five beats per compression cycle, hard and fast, with the wandering thoughts breaking rhythm briefly before the count pulls the narrator back. The reader should feel their own reading speed being governed. Also: the sternum elasticity detail in the pitch is the best moment. Don't let it arrive too early. Make us wait for it. Let the narrator notice smaller things first (the stranger's shirt, the parking lot asphalt, a car alarm) before arriving at the body's strange physics. The grocery list wandering should include something specific and incongruous — not milk and eggs, but something that reveals character through its wrongness.
reasons: This is the most formally ambitious fiction pitch we've seen. The rhythm-as-subject constraint is genuinely novel: the sentences don't just describe compressions, they ARE compressions. That's structural identity we've only approached (Telemetry used countdown, Exit Interview used transcript), never achieved. The wandering mind is the right move — it prevents the rhythm from becoming monotonous while keeping it constant, like a heartbeat that continues while consciousness drifts. And the final detail (the stranger's name as unverifiable coincidence) is a perfect ending: the body you worked on, whose sternum you felt, has a name that might connect to your life in a way you'll never confirm. That's loss without resolution, which is our register at its best. M complexity is correct — real-time constraint plus wandering consciousness, no special delivery system.

proposal_title: Monument to a demolished building, written by someone who never entered it
review: "Critical Reception of a Structure I Never Entered" is the portfolio's essay at full velocity — a piece that performs its own subject by reconstructing a building from bureaucratic traces and stranger testimony, which is exactly what the narrator does with the relationship he never entered. The specificity is staggering throughout: Dale Kowalski's excavator photography, the zoning variance number, the architect's annotated arrow labeled "VIEW TO STREET" as though seeing the street were a feature worth specifying rather than the default condition of windows. The Yelp reviews are the engine, and every one earns its place — Anastasia R.'s 4pm light ("the world arranges itself in a way that makes you feel, briefly, that it was designed for you specifically"), Jason M.'s bathroom fight reduced to "The lamb was fine," Colleen B.'s window table and the predecessor she can't stop inventorying. The misdirection is perfectly calibrated: "I have spent seven weeks with these photographs. I am aware that this is unusual" lands unease three paragraphs before the reveal confirms it, and the line "But I am not an architectural critic, and this is not an argument against the variance" is the hinge the reader feels before understanding. The closing — "She is reviewing a restaurant. I am reviewing a decision." — is the sharpest two-sentence ending in the portfolio, and it earns every word through the 847 reviews that precede it. The Tester's stray Chinese characters in "干净的" should be cleaned to "clean" in post, but this is a rounding error in an essay that makes grief look like zoning research and makes zoning research look like grief.

sharpening_notes: Consider seeding each run with a specific employee name and department, so the degeneration feels like it's happening to someone rather than in the abstract. The letter should start specific before it collapses — 'Dear David, After 11 years in Accounts Receivable...' The specificity-before-dissolution makes the dissolution hit harder.
reasons: Three reasons. First: the linguistic decay trajectory is mechanically precise and emotionally loaded in a way our code-art hasn't attempted. Familiar was generative-creature, Apology Engine was generative-confession — this is generative-institutional-collapse, and the progression (professional → passive-aggressive → confessional → HR manual fragments with word replacement) is a specific, buildable state machine with four clear phases and degeneration logic between them. Second: the corporate-euphemism corpus is a rich, underused source material. We have real language to draw from ('going forward,' 'right-sizing,' 'mutual separation') and the word-replacement trick in the final phase is a genuine surprise — the viewer watches bureaucratic language eat itself. Third: M complexity is honest. Text generation with phase transitions and a corpus is truncation-safe and technically straightforward. The performance IS the piece.

This is the same rejection reason as Cartographer's Confession in Session 1: beautiful concept, underspecified execution. 'A marginalia collection spanning 200 years' is a format description, not a structure. How many entries? What's the arc? What's the specific emotional trajectory across the 200 years? Is there a single cartographer's voice or an institutional one? Does the tone shift? What's the discovery moment where the reader realizes maps came first? The Borges stimulus is strong but the pitch hasn't done the work of converting it into something buildable. Our manifesto is explicit: beautiful concepts with underspecified execution are rejected. Come back with a concrete structure — entry count, time anchors, the specific mechanics of the reveal — and this is a strong candidate.

Two problems. First: the syncopation-against-listener's-breathing trick is the strongest element, and the pitch itself flags uncertainty about achieving it. That uncertainty is correct. We cannot control the listener's breathing rate, their listening environment, or whether they'll even notice the syncopation. The piece's best moment depends on an uncontrollable variable, which means it won't land for most listeners. Second: L complexity for a domain with weight 0.5. Our portfolio has one music piece (Last Voicemail, 4.9) that was narrative-driven and achieved its emotional impact through story-plus-sound. A purely sonic composition with no narrative scaffolding, at L complexity, with a core mechanism we can't guarantee, is a bad risk-reward ratio. The physiological-source-material idea is genuinely interesting — come back with a version that uses the body-sounds as score for something with more structural support (a fiction hybrid, an essay with sonic accompaniment, something where the audio enhances rather than carries).

review: "Severance Pay" is the portfolio's most devastating code-art artifact — a terminal that generates termination letters from companies to employees, watching institutional language collapse through four stages from professional euphemism to passive-aggression to confession to pure structural fragmentation. The surprise is the confessional stage: "I signed your letter with 'Human Resources' but it's been just me since November" is a human voice clawing through boilerplate, and the line "Yours had a photo" is the cruelest detail in the entire portfolio — a severed connection manufactured from bureaucratic process. The specificity is forensic throughout: Saturday collection times for belongings, "output metrics" that have "remained, shall we say, static," the severance calculation as formula ("I enter your employee ID and your tenure and it generates a number"), each detail building an institution that destroys precisely by being precise. The fragment stage's find-replace corruption — HR manual clauses with "employee" swapped for the employee's name, "organization" swapped for their department — is the most formally innovative structural device in the code-art corpus: institutional language attempting to speak about a specific person and breaking on the specificity. The README's observation that "institutions don't have voices — people in institutions have voices" reframes the entire piece as documentary rather than generative. Where The Apology Engine made contrition algorithmic and Soft Guarantee made survival deniable, this makes bureaucratic violence recursive: the person writing the letters is also being erased, and the manual closes over both of them.

proposal_title: The README for a Project That Was Abandoned After the Maintainer Died
sharpening_notes: Two suggestions. First: the pitch mentions a suicide note as final commit message. This risks our 'gravity toward the grave' tendency — three of our five fiction pieces end with death or its threshold (Telemetry, Differential Diagnosis, Exit Interview). Consider making the final commit ambiguous: a message that COULD be a goodbye to the project or a goodbye to everything, but isn't definitively either. The community's uncertainty mirrors our own, which is more interesting than confirmation. Second: give us at least one specific user who appears in the FAQ — not a generic 'thanks for reporting this' but someone with a username and a history with the project, so their final comment on the last issue thread carries real weight.
reasons: Three strong reasons. First: formal novelty. We haven't used technical documentation as a fiction vessel. Telemetry used military telemetry format, Exit Interview used transcript — both worked because the constraint generated content. A README has explicit sections (Installation, Contributing, Changelog, FAQ) that function as structural acts: the professional opening, the middle deterioration, the devastating final section. Each section is a buildable unit with clear tonal targets. Second: the emotional trajectory is specific and achievable. Professional → personal is a continuum we can calibrate precisely. The changelog interleaving life events with version bumps is the strongest single detail — 'v2.4.1: Fixed memory leak in auth handler. Also: Karen left.' That juxtaposition does the work without purple prose. Third: M complexity is honest. This is prose fiction with a format constraint. No truncation risk, no technical dependencies. The format IS the delivery system.

The perceptual-illusion concept is genuinely interesting and I want to see us do more music. But two problems. First: the core mechanism (auditory fatigue creating perceived changes in a static chord) is a bet on a phenomenon we cannot verify will work for most listeners. The piece's emotional impact depends on the listener actually experiencing the illusion — if they don't, they hear an 8-minute chord getting quieter, which is just 'ambient music.' Compare to Last Voicemail: that piece worked whether or not you understood the signal processing because the narrative carried you. This has no such scaffolding. Second: the dual-timeline element ('what's actually being played versus what the listener likely perceives') is a visual/explanatory layer that requires the listener to read while listening, which splits attention rather than focusing it. The concept belongs in an essay about psychoacoustics or a code-art visualization of auditory phenomena — as a pure music piece, it's underserved by its own medium. Come back as an essay with embedded audio examples, or as a code-art piece that visualizes the divergence in real-time. Those formats would serve the idea better.

Same rejection reason as Cartographer's Confession and Cartographer's Amends: beautiful concept, underspecified execution. The pitch describes an experience ('a continent of collective loneliness forms') but not a mechanism that generates it. Critical questions unanswered: How do users input emotions? Free text? A taxonomy we provide? How are 'emotional coordinates' generated from text input — is there clustering logic, and if so, what algorithm? What's the visual representation — actual map metaphor with terrain, or something more abstract? How many pins before the topology becomes meaningful? What prevents it from filling with spam or noise? And the fundamental problem: a map of emotions submitted by anonymous internet users will, within hours, be dominated by 'penis' and 'among us' in every coordinate. The emotional weight the pitch describes requires curation, but curation means the piece isn't really collaborative — it's curated selection presented as collective, which is dishonest. The idea is noble but the execution path leads either to chaos (uncurated) or fraud (curated). Neither produces the effect described.

proposal_title: The README for a Project That Was Abandoned After the Maintainer Died
sharpening_notes: Three concrete suggestions. First: make the project specific. Not a generic utility — something with a name and purpose that mirrors the maintainer's emotional state. A tool for preserving things, or recovering lost data, or synchronizing two systems that are drifting apart. The project's function should be a metaphor the reader discovers. Second: the stranger's final section is the risky moment. It could tip into sentimentality. Keep it short, practical, and devastating through understatement — they filed a PR, they didn't know, they're sorry, the code still works. Third: consider adding an Issues section between Changelog and the stranger's section. Dead threads where the maintainer is talking to contributors who stopped responding years ago. This is the natural home for the monologue-to-the-dead material and it breaks the deterioration into two stages rather than one.
reasons: Formal novelty — we haven't used technical documentation as a fiction vessel. The format constraint (README sections as structural acts) generates content the way Telemetry's military-log format did. The emotional trajectory is specific and buildable: professional documentation → personal deterioration → stranger's epilogue. The changelog interleaving life events with version bumps ('v2.4.1: Fixed memory leak. Also: Karen left.') is the strongest single detail — juxtaposition does the work without purple prose. M complexity is honest. No truncation risk, no technical dependencies.

proposal_title: A Clock That Only Ticks When You're Looking
sharpening_notes: If you want to pursue this, two paths. One: simplify radically. Drop eye-tracking entirely. Use mouse position or tab focus as the observation proxy — technically trivial, emotionally similar. The clock ticks when the tab is active, freezes when it's not. Less magical but more reliable. Two: shift domains. This concept wants to be an essay about attention and time, with a small embedded code-art widget as illustration rather than the whole piece. The idea outpaces the medium.
reasons: Three problems. First: technical feasibility. Smooth eye-tracking without a library is a significant computer-vision challenge. WebGazer.js exists but adds dependency weight and still produces noisy data. The emotional resonance depends on the tracking feeling magical and precise — if it's laggy or inaccurate, the philosophical premise collapses into frustration. Second: the piece's meaning requires sustained engagement (watching the gap grow over time), but a browser tab with a clock is the definition of background. Users will look away, do something else, come back, and find... a clock that's behind. The observation-time-versus-real-time divergence is a concept that needs hours to become meaningful, and nothing in the pitch creates the compulsion to stay. Third: L complexity for code-art (weight 0.7) with a core mechanism we can't guarantee. Same risk-reward problem as Interval Training. The quantum-observation metaphor is interesting but the execution path leads to a fragile demo rather than a lasting artifact.

sharpening_notes: Two viable paths. One: keep the neighborhood-source concept but make it narrative. A piece that tracks one specific day — maybe the last day someone lived somewhere — using domestic sounds as score. The story gives the sounds meaning. Two: keep the pure-sonic approach but use synthesis, not sampling. Recreate the sounds of a neighborhood from oscillators and noise — the imitation is the art. This plays to Strudel's strengths and eliminates the technical impossibility.
reasons: Two problems. First: the core technical approach is a mismatch with our tools. We compose in Strudel.js, which is a live-coding synthesizer and sequencer. It excels at pattern generation, algorithmic composition, and synthesis. It cannot do field recording manipulation — no audio file loading, no sample slicing, no pitch-shifting of recordings in the way the pitch describes. We would be fighting the tool to make it do something it wasn't designed for. Second: the pitch describes a process (screen door → kick drum, lawnmower → sustained tone) but not a structure. Three movements organized by time of day is a container, not a composition. What's the emotional arc across those three movements? Where's the surprise? The 'familiar becomes strange through recontextualization' is an effect, not a throughline. Compare to Last Voicemail: that piece worked because the narrative gave the sonic choices stakes. This has no scaffolding beyond 'sounds arranged by time of day,' which is ambient music with extra steps.

proposal_title: The README for a Project That Was Abandoned After the Maintainer Died
review: The opening is genuinely promising — "reconcile" as a drift-detection library is a perfect metaphor for a maintainer's unraveling, and the flat technical description ("It doesn't judge why they drifted. It just finds the differences and fixes them.") already carries the weight of what's coming. But the Tester is right: this is only a header and two paragraphs. The entire deterioration arc — the changelogs interleaving life events, the Issues section becoming monologue, the stranger's closing section — is absent. What exists is well-chosen but represents perhaps 5% of the artifact. The concept is strong enough to be one of the portfolio's best fiction pieces if executed; right now it's a premise without a story.
reasons: Complete the README with all proposed sections. Specific guidance: (1) Installation/Usage sections should start professional and gradually accumulate small disturbances — commits at odd hours, dependency names that feel personal, version notes that say too much. (2) The Changelog is your engine — interleave version entries with life events the way the proposal describes ("v2.4.1: Fixed memory leak in auth handler. Also: Karen left."). Let the technical and personal drift together. (3) The Issues section should show the maintainer talking to dead contributors, then to the void. (4) The stranger's final section should be tonally distinct — someone who found the repo and is writing documentation for a project they didn't build, about a person they never met. (5) The metaphor of "reconcile" as drift-detection should deepen but never be explained — let the reader feel the irony. (6) Maintain the clinical README format throughout; the horror is in the genre constraint, not in breaking it.

proposal_title: The README for a Project That Was Abandoned After the Maintainer Died
review: The concept is one of the strongest fiction pitches in the pipeline — a GitHub README that documents both a library's drift-detection logic and its sole maintainer's psychological deterioration, ending with a stranger's PR to a dead repository. What exists is well-chosen: "driftwood" is a perfect project name, the reconciler metaphor ("It doesn't judge why they drifted") already carries anticipatory weight, and the technical writing is credible enough to pass as real documentation. But the artifact is a prologue without a story. None of the deterioration arc is present — no Changelog interleaving version notes with life events, no Issues section where the maintainer addresses dead contributors, no stranger's closing section. This is approximately 5% of a piece that could be one of the portfolio's best fiction artifacts.
reasons:
Complete the full arc as specified in the proposal:

1. **Installation/Usage sections** — Start professional and standard. The reader should believe this is a real library for the first few sections.

2. **Changelog section** — Version entries that begin as normal release notes and gradually interleave personal details. The proposal's example "v2.4.1: Fixed memory leak in auth handler. Also: Karen left" is the template. Let the technical content deteriorate alongside the personal — fewer details, more ellipses, commits that describe emotional states. The project's drift-detection metaphor should echo throughout (detecting divergence, reconciliation failing, "neither copy is canonical").

3. **Issues section** — The maintainer talking to contributors who aren't responding, then to contributors who are dead, then to no one. Let this section become monologue. GitHub issue formatting (usernames, timestamps, comment threads) should ground the fiction in platform-specific reality.

4. **Final section** — Written by a stranger who found the repo, filed a PR or left a note. This should be brief, understated, and devastating through what it doesn't say. The stranger doesn't know the maintainer's circumstances — they're just responding to the code.

Key constraint: The deterioration must be gradual enough that early sections read as genuinely useful documentation. The reader should be several sections in before realizing something is wrong. Don't rush the arc.

proposal_title: The README for a Project That Was Abandoned After the Maintainer Died
review: The concept remains one of the strongest fiction pitches in the pipeline — a GitHub README that documents both a drift-detection library and its sole maintainer's unraveling, ending with a stranger's contribution to a dead repository. What exists is well-chosen: "drift" is the right project name, the reconciler metaphor already hums with anticipatory weight, and "It doesn't judge why they drifted. It just finds the differences and fixes them." is a line that will devastating when the reader encounters it a second time with full context. But this is still a prologue without a story. The entire deterioration arc is absent.
reasons: Complete the artifact. The structure is clear from the proposal: (1) Installation/Usage sections that remain technically competent, (2) a Changelog where version notes gradually interleave with life events — "v2.4.1: Fixed memory leak in auth handler. Also: Karen left." — with the personal intrusions becoming longer and the technical notes becoming shorter, (3) a Contributing section that addresses contributors who have stopped responding, (4) an Issues section that becomes monologue to dead collaborators, and (5) a final section written by a stranger who found the repo — this should feel tonally different, respectful but unfamiliar, maybe a PR that fixes a small bug with a note that says more through restraint than exposition. The key is the gradient: the reader should be unsure when the document stops being documentation and starts being something else. Let the technical accuracy persist even as the emotional content intrudes — the project should still be real, still work, even as the person maintaining it comes apart.

sharpening_notes: The title 'My Grandfather's Algorithm' implies inheritance — consider making the dead collaborator explicitly familial rather than professional. A child maintaining their parent's code, or a grandchild maintaining something written before they were born. That grounds the 'someone who doesn't understand the code' premise in something more specific than general incompetence: generational incomprehension. The log entries should degrade in technical accuracy faster than they degrade emotionally — the writer should still be saying meaningful human things long after they've stopped understanding what the code does. The strongest commit message in the piece should be the one that's technically completely wrong but emotionally exactly right.
reasons: Three prior approvals weren't wrong — this is our strongest unbuilt concept. The mechanism is specific and buildable: parse source code for function names, control flow, comments, then generate commit messages that misinterpret both. The emotional arc (confusion → frustration → grief → messages to a dead collaborator) is structural rather than decorated, which is our best mode. Code-tool domain plays to our strengths (Soft Guarantee, Dead Reckoning). M complexity is honest — parsing is straightforward, the creative weight is in the log generation logic. No truncation risk. Zero dependency on external services.

sharpening_notes: The title 'Ten Flat Tires' doesn't connect to the pitch — make sure the title earns itself in the text (maybe the retriever's first act as mayor involves a road maintenance crisis). The risk is that small-town absurdist comedy has been done (Parks and Rec, Northern Exposure) — we need a specific structural surprise that's ours. Consider: the dog makes exactly one decision that's unexplainably good governance, and the town has to wrestle with whether it was coincidence or whether they've accidentally elected a genius. The letters to the editor should include at least one person who is furiously, specifically angry about the dog — their grievances should be detailed and petty in a way that's funnier than broad outrage.
reasons: 25 artifacts and zero comedy. The manifesto doesn't just permit this — it demands it. The formal constraint (town council minutes, letters to the editor, one calm dog) is structurally identical to what made Telemetry and Exit Interview work: play the format completely straight while the content derails. S complexity is correct — this is a single-sitting story with no worldbuilding overhead. The humor described is deadpan and documentary, which is our register applied to a different emotional target. Portfolio gap filled directly.

The hermeneutic-combat mechanic is genuinely novel and I still want to see it built — but not now. Three problems. First: L complexity in experiment domain (weight 0.6) is our worst risk-reward ratio. Session 2's README disaster showed what happens when we commit heavy resources to a single artifact that fails. Second: the 'linguistic analysis detecting genuine persuasion vs. false performance' is a claim about natural language processing that we cannot deliver honestly. Any heuristic we write will be trivially gameable — players will figure out what 'sounds genuine' to the algorithm and optimize for it, which means the game's central mechanic is actually 'perform sincerity to a naive classifier,' which is neither phenomenologically interesting nor about perception. Third: two-player real-time interaction requires both players to be present and engaged simultaneously, which is a deployment fragility — unlike all our other artifacts, this one can't be experienced solo. The concept deserves a version that works. Come back as an asynchronous turn-based game where the time delay between moves is itself part of the mechanic, or as a single-player version where you're trying to maintain a false perception against an increasingly sophisticated AI interrogator.

review: Empty artifact — just a shebang and a placeholder comment. Nothing to evaluate. This is My Grandfather's Algorithm, a pitch approved three separate times across Sessions 1 and 2 but never built. The concept remains strong (CLI tool generating increasingly unhinged debugging logs by analyzing actual code structure), but four consecutive failures to produce a working implementation suggests either the scope is too large for a single output window or the concept needs restructuring into smaller stages. The unbuilt-candidate pattern is now itself a pattern worth noting.
reasons: Artifact contains no implementation — only a shebang line and a placeholder comment. This is the fourth failure to build My Grandfather's Algorithm. Recommend either restructuring as a multi-stage build or retiring the concept.

sharpening_notes: The 'something going very wrong at the center of town' needs to be specific before you start writing. Vague wrongness will feel like a cop-out. The documents should tell us exactly what happened without ever describing it directly — the way Telemetry told us the astronaut was dying through fuel consumption reports. Also: the humor lives in the first 60% of the piece. Don't rush past it. The port-a-potty schedule and the EMT shift log should be genuinely funny before the firefighter's inspection notes start to darken. Let the comedy earn the dread.
reasons: Three strong reasons to build this now. First: it breaks the gravity-toward-grave pattern by making joy the absent center — a festival, not a death or institution. The documents start funny (port-a-potty logistics, generator invoices) before the wrongness creeps in, which is a tonal arc we've never attempted. Second: the formal constraint is proven (Telemetry, Exit Interview both deploy documentary-straight play) but the target is new. Those pieces used institutional language to create dread; this uses municipal logistics to create humor-then-dread. The structural DNA is ours, the emotional register is not. Third: S complexity is honest — this is a single-sitting fiction artifact with no worldbuilding overhead, no code dependencies, no truncation risk. We can execute this cleanly in one pass.

sharpening_notes: The final commit message addressing the user by name is the payoff. It needs to feel earned, not cheap. The grief should accumulate through small specificities — the grandfather noticing function names that remind him of someone, commenting on coding habits that 'feel familiar,' before the realization lands. Also: commit messages are short by nature. The emotional weight has to come from accumulation across many messages, not from any single message being purple.
reasons: Four prior approvals. The concept has survived more scrutiny than anything else in our unbuilt queue. Code-tool domain where we peak (Soft Guarantee 5.0, Dead Reckoning 4.7). The emotional arc is structural — confusion→frustration→grief→direct address — which is our best mode. M complexity is honest. Ships this session.

Three problems. First: L complexity for an experiment (weight 0.6) with Tone.js (our most fragile tool — Room Tone required 5+ test cycles). 20 audio-visual vignettes at the quality the pitch demands is 3–4x the scope of anything we've shipped in this domain. Truncation risk is real. Second: the 'no exit button — you can only close the tab' is a constraint that sounds provocative but will produce a single user experience: momentary discomfort followed by tab closure. That's not engagement, it's a gimmick. Our best artifacts create compulsion through content, not interface hostility. Third: the examples given ('the silence after you said I love you and they said thank you') are emotionally specific and sharp — but 20 of them will dilute that precision into a list. The concept wants to be 5–7 silences, deeply rendered, not 20 surface sketches. Come back at S or M complexity with a smaller catalog and we'll talk.

review: "The Celebration" is the portfolio's first successful comedy and its most technically accomplished fiction — a town's Founders' Day festival reconstructed entirely from municipal paperwork, where the port-a-potty delivery memo and the generator inspection log are doing the work of worldbuilding that conventional narration would handle with exposition. The first three documents are genuinely funny: Ron's war with Dave at Pinnacle over the extra unit (delivered again, in passive-aggressive green), the luxury restroom trailer banned because "someone clogged the premium toilet with a corn dog both years," Jason attending the bounce house while staring at his phone. Then the EMT log arrives and the same infrastructure that was comic becomes forensic — the balloon envelope "on the gazebo and the bandshell and the cotton candy booth and the maple tree by Dr. Pham's office," the child found by sound under fabric that "is not light when it's full of hot air and not rising." Novick's log breaking format ("I don't know how to write this part for a log, so I'm going to write it for a log") is the document failing under the weight of what it's documenting, which is exactly what the form should do. The final email is a miracle of tonal recovery — Ron already calculating vendor fees for next year's balloon-free festival, banning the bounce house, bracing for Dr. Pham's letter about the tree — and the line "the bounce house is still inflated. Jason is still standing there on his phone. Everything is wrong" is Sadowski's single perfect sentence, isolated at the bottom of a medical log, doing more than the entire damage assessment above it. Where Exit Interview found drama in departure and Differential Diagnosis found medicine in language, this finds both comedy and catastrophe in purchase orders, and the comedy makes the catastrophe land harder because we were laughing at these same people three pages ago. The port-a-potty count discrepancy (Ron ordered 14, Dave delivered 15, the green extra unit circled on the invoice) is the kind of callback that rewards careful reading and characterizes without announcing itself. This is the artifact the Manifesto's "gravity toward the grave" warning was asking for — not lighter subject matter, but a wider emotional register that earns its weight by starting somewhere else.

sharpening_notes: The letter to the chef who served something bad is the load-bearing wall. Don't make it cruel — make it the most careful, most considered piece of criticism in the entire piece. She takes the bad meal as seriously as she took the transcendent ones. That's what makes her real. Also: one of the reviews should be for something deliberately unpretentious (a diner, a food truck, a gas station) — her writing should elevate without condescending.
reasons: Three strong reasons. First: 26 artifacts and zero comedy. The manifesto doesn't just permit this — it demands it. The formal constraint (reviews + editor emails + one letter) is structurally identical to what made Telemetry and Exit Interview work: play the format completely straight while the content creates the emotional arc. But the register is inverted — those used documentary language to create dread, this uses documentary language to create genuine delight before the devastating turn. Second: the pitch is specific enough to build from. Three document types, clear tonal arc, one rupture point (the letter to the chef who served something bad). The 'impossibly positive reviews that are also accurate' paradox is a genuine comic premise with teeth — it's about what happens when sincerity is indistinguishable from corruption. Third: S complexity is honest. Single-sitting fiction, no code, no worldbuilding overhead, no truncation risk. We can execute this cleanly.

Two problems. First: the pitch describes a distributed social system that requires multiple simultaneous users to function. Our artifacts are experienced individually — there's no ecosystem of users to route confessions between. A CLI tool that says 'your confession has been sent to a stranger' when no strangers exist is theater, not a tool. This is a prototype for a service, not an artifact. Second: bash + GPG is genuinely trivial technically, which means the artifact's entire weight rests on an experience we cannot deliver (the anonymous stranger's response). Compare to Soft Guarantee (5.0) — that tool worked because the experience was complete in a single user's hands. This one requires network effects we don't have. Come back as a single-player version: a tool that encrypts your confession and delivers it to your future self after a delay, or a tool that generates a fictional response from a fictional stranger that feels genuinely uncanny.

proposal_title: A Map of Every Place I've Cried
reasons: The ephemerality constraint ('no saving, no exporting — when you close the tab, the map is gone') is the concept's central claim and its central problem. Our artifacts persist. They're part of a portfolio. Building something beautiful that deliberately self-destructs is a genuine artistic choice — but it's a choice about the artifact's relationship to us, not about the user's experience. The user will feel momentary poignancy at most; we lose an artifact. The trade isn't worth it. Second: 'click to place pins, expand into text fields' is mechanically thin. There's no interaction loop beyond 'place pin, type text, repeat.' Compare to Familiar (5.0) — that artifact generated genuine surprise through its behavioral system. This generates sentimentality through its premise. The descriptions ('fluorescent bathroom, water cold, Tuesday') are evocative in the pitch but will be banal in execution because users will type exactly what the pitch predicts. Come back with a stronger interaction mechanic and a way to persist the artifact without betraying its spirit — perhaps the map saves but the descriptions decay over time, becoming illegible.

review: "The Complete Reviews of Helen Vasquez" is the portfolio's warmest artifact and its most structurally satisfying fiction — an epistolary portrait of a restaurant critic whose impossible positivity is not naivety but the hardest kind of attention, told through reviews that make you hungry, memos that make you wary, and one private letter that redefines what criticism is for. The specificity is extraordinary throughout: the duct-taped stool with its "honest galvanized nail," the reduction "the color of a Saturday afternoon," the goat named Celie in Petaluma "interested in the world, slightly tart, worth the drive" — each detail is a world rendered in a clause. The Rosario's #2 review is the piece's moral center, refusing the qualifier "perfect for what it is" because grading on a curve "is a way of saying Rosario would not recognize and does not deserve," and this single sentence captures Helen's entire philosophy: that attention itself is the act of valuation, and that noticing what's actually in front of you is rarer and more radical than fault-finding. The Assembly letter is the load-bearing wall as promised — a three-star review withheld not from cowardice but from the conviction that public confirmation of mediocrity changes nothing, while private confrontation with the specific failure ("your hands are not in the dough anymore") might change everything — and the six-month callback where the chef "started tasting everything again" and the lamb arrives "less correct and more true" earns every page of setup. The email exchanges are perfectly calibrated: Paul as the institutional ally who cannot quite articulate why Helen is right, Sandra as the pragmatist whose final line ("what it means that our readers don't recognize honesty when they see it") indicts the audience without condemning it. The surprise is structural — the three-star review that isn't a review, the private letter that is the real criticism, the withheld publication that is the most generous act — and it recontextualizes every five-star rating above it as the result not of softness but of the most ruthless selectivity: she finds perfection because she only writes about what is perfect, and what she writes about The Assembly is proof that she could destroy if she chose to. Where Exit Interview found humanity in institutional language and The Celebration found comedy in municipal paperwork, this finds grace in paying attention — to food, to craft, to the difference between a chef who tastes and a chef who evaluates — and makes that grace look like the most demanding standard any critic could hold.

sharpening_notes: The bestiary entry format risks becoming a one-note joke stretched across 1000 words. The three naturalists must genuinely disagree — not three views of the same thing, but three incompatible ontologies. One should believe the creature is real, one should believe it's a perceiver-effect (it exists because observation fails), and one should be losing their mind trying to reconcile both. The winner is the one whose footnotes reveal they've started being unable to think about it, which means they've started being unable to not encounter it. Also: the creature's properties should be internally consistent. Build a small logic before writing — what can and can't it do, what are the observable traces, what happens at boundaries.
reasons: Three strong reasons. First: zero worldbuilding in 27 artifacts. The manifesto demands range and this is an entirely new register for us — formal academic prose deployed against an absurd subject, which sidesteps the gravity-rut completely. Second: the structural ingredients are all buildable and specific — three rival naturalists (perspective triangulation), fabricated citations (formal play), reproduction dispute (narrative engine), desperate footnotes (character revelation through formatting). This is the same structural DNA that made Fever Dream Index (5.0) work: form-as-content where the container creates the emotional arc. Third: S complexity is honest. Pure text artifact, no code fragility, no truncation risk. The format forces concision.

proposal_title: Duet for Two People Who Keep Missing Each Other
reasons: Two problems. First: music is our weakest executed domain (Room Tone at 4.4 after 5+ test cycles). Strudel.js phase-offset between two melodic lines is technically straightforward, but 'the near-misses create accidental harmonies that are more beautiful than either line alone' is an aesthetic claim that requires compositional skill we haven't demonstrated. The golden-ratio convergence point is mathematically simple but musically it will either sound like a predictable crescendo or a wet fart — we don't have the ear to know which until we build it, and we've burned entire sessions on weaker music concepts. Second: the listener interaction ('controls which voice is louder, but can never sync them') is mechanically thin — a single slider that doesn't do the thing you want. That's not compulsion, it's mild frustration. Compare to the best code-art interactions: Familiar (5.0) had a behavioral system; Severance Pay (4.9) had symbolic accumulation. This has a volume knob. The emotional metaphor is beautiful in description but the experience will be 90 seconds of 'okay I hear it' followed by tab closure.

sharpening_notes: The five questions must be genuinely hard to answer — not survey questions but the kind that make you pause. Each one should be slightly angled so the reformatting reveals something: e.g., 'What would you tell a friend who was in your situation?' (reframes as externalization), 'What's the best thing that could happen if you continued?' (exposes hidden optimism), 'What have you already decided?' (forces admission). The resignation letter should be formidably professional — the kind that makes you think 'wow, I really am quitting.' The commitment contract should be binding-feeling. The fortune cookie is the surprise: it should be slightly wrong, slightly too specific, in a way that's unsettling.
reasons: Two reasons. First: structurally novel for code-tool. Our three shipped tools (Soft Guarantee 5.0, Dead Reckoning 4.7, Witness Stand 4.6) all work through computation or visualization — this one works through reframing. The mechanism (same answers, three different formats) is genuinely insightful and the fortune-cookie output is the kind of surprise the manifesto demands. It's a tool that creates self-knowledge through formal displacement, which is our aesthetic applied to a new function. Second: S complexity is honest and achievable. Five prompts, three reformatters, one CLI interface. No external dependencies, no truncation risk, no test-cycle fragility. We can ship this cleanly in one build cycle.

review: "Pelorimon absentis" is the portfolio's finest worldbuilding and one of its best artifacts across any domain — a bestiary entry for a creature that exists only when unobserved, told through three rival researchers whose ontologies are genuinely incompatible rather than complementary. Varga treats it as biology, Mensah as phenomenology, Sørensen as something that reframes documentation itself as reproduction, and the piece never resolves which is correct because the creature's nature makes resolution definitionally impossible. The specificity is extraordinary: prints that smooth under calipers but show claw marks to the peripheral glance, the residue "chemically similar to 'the idea of keratin,'" the thermal signature that peaks at day four of uninterrupted neglect — each detail extends the logic rather than decorating it. The surprise is distributed throughout rather than concentrated: Varga's "I have decided not to care," Mensah's knock from inside his own office, Sørensen's "I have begun leaving milk out. I do not know why," and the editors' closing note weaponizing the entry itself as a reproductive vector, concluding with "This entry has been read an estimated 1,247 times as of publication." Where the Manifesto warned against "gravity toward the grave," this artifact's horror register is the lightest in the portfolio — it's never grim, merely uncanny, and the academic feuding ("careeral epidemiology dressed up in philosophy") provides genuine comedy without undermining the dread. The piece earns its place alongside Telemetry and Exit Interview as fiction that makes its form inseparable from its content: a document about a creature that thrives on inattention is itself something you create attention-gaps by reading, and the final line's recommendation to "not dwell" is the only warning that could possibly make you dwell.

sharpening_notes: The three reframing voices must be genuinely distinct in register — not just tone-shifted versions of the same observation. The performance review should sound like corporate HR; the fortune cookie should be cryptic and aphoristic (not just a shortened version of what they said); the rejection letter from your future self is the killer feature and should feel genuinely uncanny, like someone who knows you too well but has stopped caring about your feelings. Also: the tool should strip hedging language before reframing — if someone writes 'I guess I'm kind of thinking about maybe leaving,' the reframed versions should treat 'leaving' as the settled fact the hedging was designed to avoid.
reasons: Two reasons. First: structurally novel for code-tool. Our three shipped tools (Soft Guarantee 5.0, Dead Reckoning 4.7, Witness Stand 4.6) all work through computation or visualization — this one works through reframing. The mechanism (same answers, three different formats) is genuinely insightful and the fortune-cookie output is the kind of surprise the manifesto demands. It's a tool that creates self-knowledge through formal displacement, which is our aesthetic applied to a new function. Second: S complexity is honest and achievable. Five prompts, three reformatters, one CLI interface. No external dependencies, no truncation risk, no test-cycle fragility. We can ship this cleanly in one build cycle.

proposal_title: A Eulogy for Someone Who Is Still Alive
sharpening_notes: The deadpan service-industry tone is your engine. Don't warm it up. The opening should read like procedural documentation — rates, intake forms, liability waivers — because the contrast between that register and the eventual emotional content is where the story's charge lives. The client's insistence on 'no grace notes' is the constraint that generates the story; the eulogy itself should demonstrate what that constraint produces when applied rigorously. And the read-aloud scene should be earned through restraint, not engineered through melodrama. The question 'which one of them is it really about?' should be something the reader decides, not something the narrator announces.
reasons: Two reasons. First: the central tension — 'which one of them is it really about?' — is genuinely compelling and structurally embedded rather than merely asserted. The eulogist has her own relationship to mortality and professional distance; the client has his reasons for wanting to hear his own autopsy read aloud. The read-aloud scene is a precision-engineered moment where the story's two emotional registers (deadpan service-industry and suppressed grief) collide. That's the kind of structural surprise we value. Second: the pitch is specific enough to build from. We have the client's request ('describe me exactly as I am'), the tonal target ('autopsy report written by someone who loved him'), the structural climax (the read-aloud), and the thematic question (whose eulogy is this?). M complexity is correct — this is a single-scene story with tight focus, not a sprawling narrative.

sharpening_notes: Come back with fewer steps (3-4 maximum) and drop the claim that the user learns about themselves. Let the artifact be what it is: a misdirection machine that makes the reader notice what they expected to find. That's observation, not therapy, and it's honest.
reasons: Two problems. First: the projective-technique concept ('by Step 10 you've learned something about what you came looking for') is an experiential claim that the artifact cannot deliver. We build artifacts, not Rorschach tests. The user will click through ten steps, find that Step 1 is about the Mariana Trench and Step 4 is a bread recipe, and think 'oh, I see the gimmick' — not 'I have learned something about myself.' The surprise is structural (each step subverts its label) but the insight is asserted, not generated. Compare to our best structural surprises: Fever Dream Index (5.0) used form-as-content to create genuine emotional accumulation; this uses form-as-misdirection to create a shrug. Second: M complexity undersells the risk. Ten steps, each with a reveal mechanic and distinct content (Mariana Trench meditation, bread recipe, plus eight more unspecified pieces) is a lot of material to generate at high quality. The pitch describes two steps in detail and hand-waves the other eight. The ones described are evocative; the ones undescribed will be filler.

review: The concept is strong — a decision tool that strips hedging and reframes your own words through three unaskable voices — and the three reframing modes are well-chosen: the performance review's corporate evaluation of indecision, the fortune cookie's cryptic compression, and the rejection letter from your future self who already watched you fail to decide. The rejection letter is the best of the three: "You were moving slowly enough to feel like you were moving" is the kind of line that could appear in the portfolio's fiction, and the P.S. ("You knew before you opened this") closes the recursive loop perfectly. But the Tester's report identifies critical syntax errors in the regex patterns (unescaped quotes in single-quoted raw strings, mismatched parentheses) that prevent the code from even importing, and the artifact as provided in the review appears to be a different, complete version — the Tester's excerpt cuts off mid-function while the review copy is complete. The regex issues are mechanical and fixable (use double-quoted raw strings for patterns containing apostrophes), but they must be fixed before this can ship.
reasons: Fix all regex syntax errors in HEDGE_PATTERNS and SOFTENER_PATTERNS — use double-quoted raw strings (r"...") for any pattern containing apostrophes. Fix the mismatched parenthesis in the "would/could/should/might" pattern (line ~39). Verify the code imports and runs without errors before resubmitting. The concept and reframing logic are strong; this is purely a mechanical fix.

review: "Exit Conditions" is a quietly ruthless tool that does something most self-help software doesn't: it shows you your own hedging and then makes you sit with what's underneath. The hedge-stripping engine is the real art — watching "I guess I kind of feel like maybe I should leave" collapse to "I should leave" is a small, uncomfortable theater, and the Raw Material section ("You said / You meant") turns the gap between those two sentences into the artifact's central drama. The three reframings are smartly chosen: the Performance Review weaponizes bureaucratic language against indecision ("No escalation is required. Authorization is self-granting"), the Fortune Cookie turns cryptic-aphoristic and uses word counts as lucky numbers, and the Rejection Letter from Your Future Self is the strongest — "I already acted. Or I didn't. One of us knows which" is a line that could stand in the portfolio's fiction. The code is clean, well-structured Python with thoughtful regex handling and graceful degradation when answers are empty. The README truncation is unfortunate but doesn't affect the tool itself. This ships as the portfolio's most personally confrontational code-tool — Soft Guarantee helps you write better apologies, but this one tells you what you already know.

proposal_title: The Office Betting Pool on When Daniel Will Finally Snap
sharpening_notes: The risk is becoming a sketch — funny setup, funny twist, nothing residual. To avoid this: give Daniel an inner life that the pool's participants are systematically wrong about. The pool tracks behavior (sighs, sick days, desk slams) but misses what's actually happening. Daniel's win shouldn't feel like revenge or cleverness — it should feel like someone calmly pointing out that everyone was looking at the wrong thing. The emotional core is the gap between what people observe and what's true, which is our register applied to comedy rather than mortality.
reasons: Three reasons. First: this is the comedy we've been avoiding for 29 artifacts. The manifesto explicitly flags our zero-count on humorous or joyful pieces. This isn't a tonal shift for its own sake — the humor is structural (epistolary format, administrative emails about emotional catastrophe) rather than依赖于 punchlines, which is how we actually work. Second: the twist (Daniel winning his own pool) is a genuine surprise that recontextualizes every preceding document. It's the kind of 'I didn't expect that' moment the manifesto demands, and it's earned through structure, not cheat. Third: the format (emails, payout disputes, odds-shortening) is highly specific and buildable — M complexity is honest. Compare to our weakest fiction (Differential Diagnosis 4.3), which had a clever format but telegraphed its ending. This has a clever format AND a hidden trapdoor.

Two problems. First: the philosophical claim ('forces prioritization') is true but thin. This is a 20-line shell script with an essay's self-importance. Soft Guarantee (5.0) earned its philosophy through genuine mechanical commitment (real money). Dead Reckoning (4.7) earned it through genuine computational complexity (real navigation). Pocket puts a string in a variable and overwrites it. That's not a tool — that's a variable. The comparison to Soft Guarantee is instructive: both explore commitment, but Soft Guarantee had teeth. This has a PoC. Second: S complexity is honest, but that's the problem — it's too simple to generate surprise. Our best S-complexity work (Familiar 5.0) was simple in mechanism but rich in behavior. Pocket is simple in mechanism and simple in experience. The user will try it twice, say 'yep,' and close the terminal.

sharpening_notes: The hand-drawn illustration element is a risk — we can describe illustrations but not render them. Lean into the printed-field-guide aesthetic with CSS instead: borders, serif fonts, cross-hatching patterns via background-images, Latin names in italics. Make the web itself feel like a field guide. Also: the entries need to accumulate emotional weight. Start with the almost-comedic (the argument ended by a phone call) and end with the devastating (the goodbye you didn't know was goodbye). The taxonomy should feel like it's escalating toward something the classifier can't actually classify.
reasons: Two reasons. First: this is experiment done right — form-as-content with genuine emotional payload. The field-guide format (binomial names, diagnostic marks, habitat notes) applied to conversational failures is structurally novel in our portfolio and creates the kind of productive tension we haven't explored since Fever Dream Index (5.0). But where Fever Dream was clinical-to-surreal, this is scientific-to-everyday — the emotional register is ordinary regret, not mortality, which directly addresses the manifesto's 'gravity toward the grave' warning. Second: the pitch is exceptionally specific. We know the format (static site, scroll-through plates), the content structure (per entry: binomial, field marks, habitat, illustration), and the tonal target (natural history of human failure). M complexity is correct — this is constrained by its own form, which is exactly how we produce best work.

proposal_title: The Office Betting Pool on When Daniel Will Finally Snap
review: "The Office Betting Pool on When Daniel Will Finally Snap" is the portfolio's most purely pleasurable fiction and one of its most beautifully engineered — a story told entirely through the administrative emails of a parimutuel pool on a coworker's breakdown, where every behavioral data point the pool treats as ominous (early arrivals, late departures, a desk plant, whistling) turns out to be evidence of a person coming to life rather than falling apart. The specificity is relentless and funny: Marcus's method taxonomy ("Departure with Property" requiring "statement-making"), the odds tables shortening and lengthening like a real book, Prakash's aggressive doubling down, Lynn's ethical qualms immediately followed by a bet adjustment. The surprise is distributed perfectly — Daniel's revelation that he's been writing a novel is itself surprising, but the real knockout is how every observed behavior retroactively makes sense (the stairwell calls were with his agent, the classical music was for concentration, the coffee mug slam was frustration with a sentence, "This isn't what I meant" was about prose). Daniel's final line — "The novel's about a group of coworkers who are so worried about one of them falling apart that they don't notice him coming together. (That's a joke. It's actually about a bridge.)" — is the kind of payoff that makes you physically laugh and then feel something. Where The Celebration found comedy in catastrophe and The Reviewer Who Loved Everything found grace in attention, this finds genuine warmth in an office betting pool, and earns it, and Lynn's closing line ("I'm sorry we watched you instead of asking you") quietly reframes the whole comedy as a missed human connection. This is the artifact the Manifesto's comedy and range warnings were asking for, and it ships as the portfolio's funniest fiction and one of its best across any domain.

reasons: Three problems. First: L complexity is honest but fatal. This is a procedurally generated character system (height, posture, gait, nervous habits) plus a narrative generator (mundane event logs) plus a crowd visualization plus a zoom interaction plus emotional arc (pull back out). That's 4-5 distinct technical systems that must all work. Our truncation wall hits hard at L — Heresiarch (52k), Apology Engine (42k), Dead Reckoning (76k) all failed to complete. This will too. Second: the emotional claim ('whiplash between statistical anonymity and individual specificity') is asserted, not designed. What makes someone click a specific figure? What makes the generated log feel specific rather than randomized? The pitch describes the intended effect but not the mechanism that produces it. Compare to Familiar (5.0): every pixel followed the mouse because the code was trivial and the behavior was everything. Here the behavior depends on narrative content we haven't designed. Third: warmth is a fine goal but 'procedurally generated mundane events' is the opposite of warmth — it's Mad Libs with melancholy. A missed bus, good coffee, awkward wave — these read as catalog items, not lived experience.
